raw_response:
I'm a 52-year-old woman farming 12 mu in Quzhou County. I've been at this for about 5 years now—not long enough to feel like I really know everything, but long enough to have learned a few hard lessons. My husband and one of my sons work off-farm in the county town, so most days it's just me and my daughter-in-law handling the fields, with my son coming back for busy times like harvest and planting. We need the off-farm income—farming 12 mu alone won't pay for everything—but it means we're short on labor when things get tight.

I just got the summer maize in the barn last week, and now I'm turning my mind to the winter wheat. October 10th is my target for planting. Last year I planted a bit late because the maize harvest dragged, and I think the wheat suffered for it—yield was down maybe 30 kg per mu compared to the year before. So this year I'm determined to get it in on time, even if I have to hire a couple days of help to get the fields ready.

For seed, I'll use the same improved variety I bought last year from the seed dealer in town. I saved some seed from my own harvest but I don't trust it as much—heard from my neighbor that saved seed doesn't vigor as well, and I can't afford a bad stand. It costs about 40 yuan per mu for the seed, which is a lot, but I budgeted for it.

Fertilizer is where I always worry about money. The extension fellow told me 15 kg of nitrogen per mu is about right for my soil, and I usually do close to that. This year I'm thinking 16 kg N per mu for the wheat—I use a compound fertilizer as base (about 50 kg per mu of the 15-15-15 stuff, which gives me some P and K too), and then I'll topdress with urea at green-up and again at jointing if the wheat looks hungry. I usually do two fertilizer applications, sometimes three if the spring is dry and the wheat looks yellow. Last year I only topdressed once because fertilizer prices were high, and I regretted it. This year prices came down a bit, and my son sent some money home, so I can afford the extra urea.

Irrigation for wheat—I'll definitely water three times if I can afford the electricity. The well water isn't free anymore; they meter it now and it adds up. But wheat pays the bills around here. I'll irrigate at overwintering if it's dry, definitely at jointing in March-April, and once more at grain filling in May if there's no rain. My neighbor Wang only does two times and his yields are always a bit lower, so I figure the extra water pays for itself.

For the maize next June—well, that's a long way off, but I know the drill. I'll plant hybrid seed right after wheat harvest, probably June 12th or 13th if the wheat comes off clean. The window is brutal—sometimes only five or six days. I'll hire a custom operator with a planter because there's no way I can plant 12 mu by hand in that heat and time. For fertilizer, I usually put down about 45 kg per mu of compound at planting, which gives me around 14-15 kg N per mu. I might topdress once at the big flare if the season looks good. Irrigation for maize—maybe once or twice. The summer rains usually help, and honestly, by August I'm watching every yuan. If the maize looks okay and it rained, I'll skip the second irrigation. 

Pesticides—I'll spray herbicide on the wheat once in the spring for weeds, and probably a fungicide too because last year there was some rust in the village. For maize, I usually just do a pre-emergent herbicide and that's it unless I see borers. My daughter-in-law helps with spraying; we have an old backpack sprayer.

Labor: For wheat, I figure about 15 family days across the season—planting, fertilizing, spraying, irrigating, harvest. I'll hire about 5 days for the heavy stuff and combining. For maize, maybe 10 family days and 8 hired days because the June turnaround and September harvest are so rushed.

I expect about 480 kg per mu from the wheat if things go well—last year I only got 420 because of the late planting and dry spring. For maize, I'm hoping 520 kg per mu, which is what my brother-in-law usually gets.
